note: The address and greeting in 1–3 lead into thanksgiving for gifts and confidence about the future.
Paul recalls the few people he baptized in verses 14–16 and qualifies his recollection. Verse 17 states how he understands his commission.
The cross reverses ordinary evaluations of power. The appeal to the Corinthians' own calling supplies a second argument against boasting.
Paul gives a reason for his manner of preaching in Corinth.
The hidden wisdom claim leads to an account of disclosure and then to a distinction between ways of hearing it.
The milk metaphor interprets rivalry between factions. Agricultural, building and temple images successively describe the community.
The hardships illustrate the appeal to imitation. Timothy's coming and the prospect of a disciplinary visit give the closing challenge its setting.
A reported relationship prompts the assembly's disciplinary action. The yeast and Passover images then extend the appeal to collective conduct.
The litigation questions culminate in a challenge to accept loss. The inheritance warning and reminder of washing address the same audience.
Permission sayings and replies precede the argument about bodily union. Quotation marks in an English edition leave the original speaker open.
Verse 1 introduces the Corinthians’ letter. The abstinence maxim may voice their position. The referent of the concession in 6 is disputed. Verses 8–9 address unmarried people and widows.

Verse 10 names the Lord as authority. Verse 11 includes a parenthetical direction. Verse 12 introduces Paul’s ruling on a different case. Verse 15 permits departure. Whether it also permits remarriage remains disputed.
Circumcision illustrates calling in 17–19. Verses 20–24 turn to enslaved and free people. The object implied in the imperative in 21 remains interpretively disputed.
Verse 25 introduces personal judgment in the absence of a command from the Lord. Verses 29–35 give reasons. The relationship in 36–38 is disputed. Verse 40 again marks personal judgment.
Love and knowledge frame the argument. Verses 4–6 have a separate overlapping indexed parent. Verses 7–8 qualify the implied consensus about idols.
The concession about so-called gods introduces the first-person plural confession of one God and one Lord.
Rhetorical questions, an embedded Torah citation in 9, and the temple analogy precede the Lord-attributed ruling in 14. Paul explains in 15–18 why he waives the right.
Paul first describes adapting his practice. The athletic illustration in 24–27 addresses perseverance and includes Paul himself.
Israel's wilderness experiences become examples for the readers. The final assurance about temptation qualifies the preceding warning.
The incompatibility of ritual tables precedes case-specific advice about buying food or accepting hospitality.
The speaker asks the recipients to imitate his example insofar as he imitates Christ. The imperative continues the preceding argument.

The record for verse 5 isolates evidence of women praying and prophesying within the larger covering instruction in 4–6. Verses 11–12 qualify the preceding appeal to origins. The meaning of head and the appeal to angels require further review.

Paul addresses divisions and hunger before citing the supper. Verse 23 frames the tradition, 24–25 report words over bread and cup, and 26 supplies an explanation. Verse 34 closes with a local meal instruction and defers other matters to a visit.
The opening recalls the readers' former practices. Verse 3 gives contrasting speech tests concerning Jesus.
The distribution of gifts brackets the body analogy. The questions in verses 29–30 expect different functions among the members.
Hypothetical speech, knowledge and sacrifice introduce the description of love and the discussion of what endures.

Tongues and prophecy are evaluated in terms of intelligibility, edification and the visitor. Verse 21 introduces a scriptural citation voiced by the Lord. Verses 22–25 are Paul’s argument about its implications.

Assembly directions are interrupted by the contested restriction separately indexed under 34–35. Verse 36 challenges the audience. Verse 37 claims divine authority for written directions. The referent of those directions requires interpretation.

The received text contains the restriction. Its manuscript position, possible interpolation and proposal that it voices a position answered in 36 are distinct questions. Speaker attribution remains disputed.
Paul marks the proclamation as received and delivered. The appearance to himself leads to an account of his own calling.
The consequences of denying resurrection precede the firstfruits image, the order of resurrection and the handing over of the kingdom.
Baptism for the dead appears as a premise in a question. Paul gives no instructions for performing it.
A posed objection introduces analogies for bodily change. The closing imperative connects resurrection hope with present labor.
The collection instructions specify regular saving and representatives approved by the recipients.
Travel intentions are conditional. Directions about Timothy and recognizing service accompany a distinct series of short exhortations.
Greetings from Asia and from a house assembly identify hosts and contacts. The verse gives no instruction about who should lead.
Mutual greeting, the writer's signature, a warning and invocation, and the final blessing and expression of love have distinct functions.
Senders and addressees exchange a conventional greeting.
Thanksgiving recalls how the Thessalonians responded to the message.
The writers defend their conduct by recalling their work and their relationship with the recipients.
The writers compare two communities under pressure. The polemical accusation in 14–16 requires historical and textual review before wider application.
2:17–18 and 3:1–2, 5–7 explain the separation, Timothy's visit and his return. The visit gives the exhortation about suffering its setting.

The writers appeal to instructions given through the Lord Jesus in 1–2. The exhortation that follows is in their collective voice. The interpretation of the expression translated as control of the body in 4 requires Greek review.
The writers distinguish the recipients’ existing practice of love from their appeal for further growth, quiet conduct, and work.
Grief supplies the setting. Verse 15 invokes a word of the Lord about priority. Its possible scope extends into 16–17. Verse 18 turns to mutual consolation.
The thief and labor-pain comparisons in 2–3 concern timing. In 4–8 the writers address vigilance. In 9–11 Christ’s death grounds hope and mutual encouragement.

12–13 concerns those who work among the assembly and peace within it. Verse 14 differentiates the needs of recipients. In 15 the prohibition of retaliation extends beyond the community. In 19–22 openness to prophecy is paired with testing.

23 is a prayer and 24 expresses confidence in the one who calls. 25–27 request prayer, a greeting and public reading. Verse 28 gives the final grace wish. The solemn instruction to read in 27 is the writer’s own.
The letter introduces its claimed sender, invokes divine authorization and greets Timothy. Its Pauline authorship is disputed.
3–7 connects opposition to speculative teaching with the positive goal of love. The list in 9–10 illustrates the use of law and includes slave traders.
The autobiographical voice frames a traditional saying and then addresses Timothy. Verse 20 supplies named examples of the warning.
Prayers for rulers serve the stated aim of a quiet life. Verses 3–6 ground the appeal in a universal saving desire and one mediator. Verse 7 adds the speaker's claim to teach Gentiles.
8 addresses men praying. 9–10 contrast expensive display and good works. 11–12 regulate women's learning and teaching. The creation appeal and difficult childbearing statement follow in 13–15.
The household analogy in 4–5 is part of the case for overseer qualifications. The women in 11 may be wives or women serving. WEBP's choice of wives does not settle the office question.
14–15 explain why instructions are being written ahead of a possible visit. Verse 16 shifts to a confessional sequence. Its opening wording requires comparison across editions.
1 introduces a prediction as speech of the Spirit. The letter describes rival restrictions in 2–3 and gives its own theological answer about creation and thanksgiving in 4–5.
The exercise comparison in 7–8 supports training in godliness. Public reading, exhortation and teaching in 13 are distinct from the personal gift and persistence in 14–16.
1–2 directs Timothy to address different ages as kin. The subsequent rules distinguish household care, enrollment with age and conduct criteria, and aid for widows without support.

Verse 18 introduces two citations as Scripture, including a laborer's entitlement to pay. It does not name Jesus as speaker. The writer shifts from impartial discipline to caution about laying on hands, an individual health suggestion and the visibility of deeds.
Enslaved people are addressed in both verses. The second case concerns believing masters. The letter preserves this social relation while invoking shared faith.
The author invokes teaching associated with the Lord Jesus in 3, then criticizes disputes and the treatment of religion as a source of profit. No saying from Jesus is quoted.
The warning in 6–10 concerns contentment and the desire for wealth. Timothy is addressed personally in 11–16. Instructions to those already rich begin in 17 and direct them to share.
Timothy is charged to guard a deposit and avoid contrary claims to knowledge. A grace wish closes the letter.
Apostolic self-identification, co-sender, recipients and greeting introduce the correspondence.
The opening blessing connects received and shared comfort. The affliction in Asia illustrates reliance on God and the recipients' participation in prayer.
Verses 12–17 defend the writers' conduct and changed itinerary. Verse 23 invokes God as witness to the explanation for the delayed visit.
The account explains why Paul wrote instead of returning for another painful visit. His aim in writing is explicit in verse 4.
The punishment by the majority is treated as sufficient. Paul requests comfort, forgiveness and reaffirmation of love.
12–13 recount travel and anxiety about Titus. The argument changes to thanksgiving in 14.
The letter metaphor addresses ministerial credentials. The veil imagery interprets Moses and leads into the claim about transformation.
The argument moves from open proclamation through bodily vulnerability to the grounds for hope amid suffering.
Dwelling and clothing images frame the hope of life. Confidence before death leads into accountability before Christ.
The account of persuasion and motives leads into the implications of one person's death for all, new creation and the appeal for reconciliation.
A scriptural citation introduces the appeal concerning grace. The ministry catalogue supports the request for mutual openness.
6:14–16a argues by paired questions. From the citation formula in 16b the first person is God's voice within scripture. The letter resumes its own voice at 7:1.
Titus's arrival and report frame the distinction between kinds of grief and the expression of renewed confidence.
Macedonia supplies an example. Paul distinguishes advice from command and relates completion of the collection to the donors' means.
The delegates are commended through their service and selection by assemblies. Their names are supplied only for Titus.
Advance preparation protects the voluntary character of the gift. Material relief and thanksgiving to God are both named as outcomes.
The challenge about letters and personal presence belongs to a defense of authority. The limits of boasting concern the writers' own field of labor.
The account of financial support is part of Paul's defense against rival apostles and his warning about a different proclamation.
Paul introduces ironic boasting in 16–21. The catalogue in 22–29 and escape narrative in 31–33 give the concrete content of his boast.
The vision narrative withholds the words heard in 4. The answer in 9a is reported divine speech in response to prayer. Paul resumes in 9b and draws the inference in 10.
Paul defends apostolic signs, recalls financial conduct and reports concern about his visit. Verse 16 entertains an accusation before the rebuttal in 17–18.
The witness citation and threat of discipline frame the demand for proof. Prayer for restoration and a closing greeting precede the blessing.
Joint sender formula, address and wish for grace and peace.
Thanksgiving for endurance in 3–5 leads to the expectation of relief and divine recompense in 6–10. In 11–12 the writers pray for the recipients' calling and actions.
The addressees have heard claims that the day has arrived, possibly in a letter ascribed to the writers. The restraining power in 6–7 is left unnamed. The sequence ends with deception and judgment.
Thanksgiving for the recipients gives way to the instruction in 15 to hold teachings received by speech or letter. 16–17 invoke encouragement from Jesus and the Father.
The request for prayer concerns the spread of the message and rescue from opponents. The writers express confidence in 3–4 and pray for the direction of their readers' hearts in 5.

The economic maxim in 10 is recalled as the writers' own earlier directive. It concerns unwillingness to work. The instruction to limit association in 14 is qualified by treating the person as a brother in 15.
Verse 17 claims an autograph sign. Verse 18 closes with a grace wish.
The opening address in 1–2 precedes prayerful recollection of a particular family's faith.

A gift recalled through laying on hands leads to the summons to share suffering. In 9–12 the writer connects calling and grace with his own imprisonment. The Spirit appears again in the instruction to guard the deposit.
The report of desertion in 15 contrasts with a named visitor's care in 16–18.

The charge to transmit teaching stands between a call to draw strength from grace and three vocational comparisons. The confession in 11–13 is introduced as a trustworthy saying without naming its author.
The teaching that resurrection has already happened in 18 is attributed to named opponents. Verse 19 responds with a foundation bearing two sayings. Household vessels form a new comparison in 20–21.
Pursuit of virtues and refusal of quarrels frame gentleness toward opponents. The desired repentance in 25 depends on divine action.
A list of vices warns about the last days. The comparison with Jannes and Jambres in 8–9 interprets the conduct of the particular teachers being attacked.
Timothy's knowledge of the speaker's conduct and suffering precedes the appeal to childhood knowledge of Scripture. Its functions in 16–17 culminate in readiness for good work.
1–2 give a charge before God and Christ; the predicted resistance in 3–5 is its setting. In 6–8 the voice looks back on a completed race and ahead to a crown also for others.
9–13 and 19–22 concern travel, supplies, colleagues and greetings. The account of the defense includes a prayer for those who deserted the speaker.
Sender, co-sender, recipients and grace greeting.
The report from Epaphras in 7–8 connects thanksgiving to intercession.
The Son is the subject throughout. Creation and powers in 15–17 lead to headship, resurrection, and reconciliation in 18–20. The chapter does not identify a prior hymn or its composer.
21–23 apply reconciliation to the recipients and call for persistence. In 24–29 the writer interprets his suffering, commission and labor to present others mature.
The speaker describes concern for people he has not met and explains the danger of plausible arguments. The instruction to continue as they received Christ begins at 6.
8 warns about deceptive arguments. 9–15 connect Christ, baptism and the defeat of powers. The prohibitions in 21 illustrate regulations the writer challenges; they are not his instructions.
1–4 connect conduct with rising with Christ. 5–11 oppose former practices and describe a renewed humanity. The appeal to forgive in 12–15 is followed by instruction through song and gratitude.
The writer addresses wives and husbands, children and fathers, then enslaved workers. The corresponding address to masters occurs beyond the chapter boundary at 4:1.
Verse 1 concludes the household directions begun in chapter 3. The instructions then turn to prayer for proclamation and to speech with outsiders.
Travel news and named greetings frame local requests. Epaphras's prayer is reported in 12. Verse 18 closes with a request to remember the writer's chains.
Sender and audience formula followed by a grace and peace greeting.
The blessing links adoption with praise, redemption with the divine purpose, and inheritance with the seal of the Spirit. The movement between we and you is relevant to the audience.
A prayer for understanding develops into claims about Christ's authority.
The former condition and divine mercy in 1–7 set up the relation between grace, faith and good works in 8–10. The writer distinguishes the basis of salvation from its intended result.
Gentile exclusion in 11–12 precedes nearness through Christ. The dividing barrier and cross in 14–18 explain the shared citizenship, household and temple images in 19–22.
The revealed mystery is given concrete content in 6 as Gentile co-inheritance. The first-person ministry account ends with an appeal concerning the writer's suffering in 13.
The prayer moves from petition to praise at verse 20.
The appeal to unity includes a sequence of shared commitments in 4–6. A citation and its interpretation in 7–10 lead into distinct ministries and their common purpose in 11–16.
The writer contrasts a stereotyped account of Gentile conduct with learning Christ and putting on a new self. This is a polemical appeal to the readers about their conduct.
Truthfulness, anger, labor and sharing lead into speech that builds others up. The final appeal grounds forgiveness in God's forgiveness in Christ.
Christ's self-giving grounds imitation in 1–2. The quoted summons to wake in 14 sits inside the light imagery; its precise source is unstated. Wisdom, singing and thanksgiving follow.

The move from mutual submission in 21 to the directions to wives and husbands matters to interpretation. The quotation in 31 and its Christ-and-assembly application in 32 are part of the writer's analogy.
The instruction to children invokes the commandment to honor parents and its promise. Verse 4 directly addresses fathers about provoking and bringing up children.
The first address is to enslaved people. Verse 9 addresses masters, prohibits threats and appeals to their common heavenly master. The passage does not prescribe emancipation.
The armor simile specifies the opponents as spiritual powers. Prayer extends the appeal beyond the addressees to all the saints and to the writer's speech in chains.
21–22 commend Tychicus as messenger. The final blessing specifies its recipients.
The salutation makes claims about the origin of apostleship and the purpose of Christ's death.
13–24 narrate Paul's earlier persecution, calling and travels in support of his claim about the origin of his gospel.
1–2 set the Jerusalem meeting. Titus supplies a concrete test in 3–5. Recognition of distinct missions in 6–9 precedes the request about the poor. Paul recounts what others asked him in 10.

Paul narrates the withdrawal at Antioch and supplies his challenge to Peter in 14. How far the reported speech continues after 14 is uncertain. The argument about justification remains Paul's voice under either reading.
Paul questions the readers about how they received the Spirit, then cites Abraham and the promise to the nations. Scripture personified as speaking in 8 introduces a scriptural promise.
The argument links several scriptural citations about doing, living and curse. In 13–14 Christ bearing the curse leads to the Gentile blessing and reception of the Spirit.
A ratified covenant and the singular offspring ground Paul's chronological argument. In 19 and 21 he poses distinct questions about why the law was given and whether it opposes the promises.
Custody and the guardian comparison are temporal in Paul's argument. The next parent begins his explanation about children of God.
Baptism leads into the named pairs and Abrahamic inheritance. The explicit claim is shared belonging in Christ; the passage does not specify changes in civil status.
Minor heirs under guardians introduce adoption and the Spirit's cry in 6. Paul then challenges observance of calendrical cycles and fears his work may be wasted.
Paul recalls illness and welcome in 13–15 and expresses distress in 19–20.
Paul calls his treatment of the two women allegorical. The citation in 30 is part of his application to the addressees; it is not presented as an instruction from Jesus.
A command to stand firm applies the preceding contrast between freedom and slavery and anticipates the warning about circumcision.
Paul warns a person accepting circumcision about the obligation involved. The hope of righteousness through the Spirit precedes his conclusion about faith acting in love in 6.
The race and yeast images address interference with the readers. Paul links persecution to the cross and ends with a bitter wish directed at the agitators.
Freedom is the occasion for service in love. Verse 14 cites the neighbor command from Scripture without attributing these words to Jesus.
The warning about mutual destruction applies the preceding appeal for love to conduct inside the community.
Spirit-led conduct is contrasted with desire and a vice list. The fruit list in 22–23 leads to an exhortation against rivalry and envy in 25–26.

Restoring another person and bearing burdens precede a distinct call for self-examination and responsibility in 3–5. Verse 6 concerns material sharing with a teacher. The sowing image introduces perseverance in 7–10.
The handwriting notice in 11 introduces the circumcision polemic. The writer shifts to boasting in the cross, new creation, a peace wish, marks borne on his body and a closing blessing.
1–3 name the household audience. The thanksgiving anticipates the personal appeal later in the letter.

The writer explicitly appeals to Philemon’s voluntary action in 8–14, asks him to welcome Onesimus in 15–17, and personally offers to cover a possible debt in 18–21. The conditional debt is no proof that Onesimus stole. The letter leaves the legal outcome unstated.
A personal lodging request, expectation of release through prayer, greetings and closing blessing concern the immediate visit and correspondents.
Co-senders address the community, including overseers and servants. Their mention supplies evidence about addressees without prescribing offices.
Thanksgiving and prayer precede prison news. Paul reflects on mixed preaching motives and weighs death against continued service.
The appeal for common conduct in 27 develops into a contrast of outcomes in 28. The reference to suffering in 29–30 concerns the Philippians’ shared struggle.

A communal appeal against rivalry leads to Christ as example in 5. Humiliation and obedience in 6–8 are answered by exaltation and universal homage in 9–11. The passage does not identify the prior origin of its wording.
The addressees are plural in 12. Divine action in 13 grounds the appeal. Verses 14–16 concern conduct and the word of life. In 17–18 the offering image leads to an appeal for shared joy.

Travel plans and illness reports explain the recommendations of Timothy and Epaphroditus. On 2026-11-28 verses 25–28 were inspected again and retained as a narrative example of shared distress and relief. The command to welcome the coworker follows in 29–30.

The call to rejoice introduces a polemical warning in 2–3. Paul recounts credentials in 4–6 before reassessing their worth in 7–11. The exact force of the faith expression in 9 requires a Greek review.
Paul describes pressing forward in 12–14 and asks the mature to share his outlook in 15–16. The competing examples in 17–19 precede the collective hope of transformation in 20–21.
The appeal to stand firm follows the expectation of transformation in 3:20–21.
Paul addresses Euodia and Syntyche by name and asks a third party to help. Their past mission work is explicit. The object of their disagreement is unstated.
Joy and gentleness in 4–5 precede prayer with thanksgiving in 6. Verse 7 describes the promised protection of God’s peace.
The list of qualities for reflection in 8 is followed by an instruction to practice what the recipients learned and observed in 9.
Paul describes hunger as well as abundance before the strength claim in 13. Verses 14–18 acknowledge particular gifts. The assurance of provision in 19 and praise in 20 close the acknowledgment.
An instruction to convey greetings, reciprocal greetings and a final blessing close the letter.
The opening address contains a compressed gospel formulation. In 8–15 a proposed visit introduces mutual encouragement and the scope of Paul's mission.
The claim about the gospel's power for Jew and Greek precedes Paul's appeal to the written saying about faith and life.
The repeated language of giving people over connects idolatry, passions and the concluding list. The address turns to the person judging in 2:1.
The second-person challenge addresses someone who condemns conduct they also practice. Divine kindness introduces the appeal to repentance.
Paul joins impartiality to judgment according to deeds, then considers people with and without the law.
A series of questions tests the claim to teach the law. The argument then turns from circumcision to obedience and the heart.
Objections and replies introduce a chain of scriptural citations. Verses 19–20 draw the conclusion about law and accountability.
The claim about the law and prophets' witness frames the subsequent claims about grace, redemption and divine justice.
A brief question and reply on boasting links the preceding argument to the claim about justification in verse 28.
The one-God argument concerns circumcised and uncircumcised alike. Verse 31 answers an objection about nullifying the law.
Abraham and David supply scriptural examples. The timing of circumcision grounds the argument about Abraham's wider family.
The promise to Abraham, his trust despite bodily circumstances, and the application to people who believe in the God who raised Jesus form successive units.
The first-person plural argument moves from hope in distress to Christ's death for sinners and reconciliation of enemies.
The comparison with Adam includes a qualification about law and death, then several contrasts between trespass and gift.
A question about continuing in sin introduces baptismal participation in death and resurrection. Direct imperatives conclude the passage.
The writer explicitly calls the slavery imagery a human analogy. The passage contrasts outcomes of obedience and sin.
The illustration of a married woman's relation to law sets up Paul's application about belonging to the risen Christ.
The prohibition of coveting is quoted within a first-person account of the relation between sin and commandment.
The first-person speaker dramatizes conflict. Identifying the speaker historically or theologically requires further interpretation.
Freedom from condemnation introduces the argument about God's action through the Son and the law's requirement.
The contrast between flesh and Spirit leads to claims about bodily life, adoption and shared suffering with Christ.
Creation's groaning and the Spirit's intercession are distinct. The final questions and scriptural citation express confidence amid threats.
Personal grief introduces the discussion of Israel. Scriptural speakers are embedded in Paul's replies about election, mercy and the remnant.
Paul moves from a question to scriptural warrant, then prayer and explanation. His explicit desire for Israel's salvation qualifies how the accusation is read.
The one-verse claim about Christ and the law follows 9:30–10:3. An English rendering alone leaves the interpretation of telos open.
Scripture is reapplied to confession and calling, the sequence of sending and hearing, and the response of Israel.
Paul invokes his own ancestry and the Elijah narrative before addressing Gentile readers through the grafting image.
The warning against conceit leads into Israel's future and mercy. A doxology closes the argument.
The appeal about bodies and minds introduces humble self-assessment and the differentiated use of gifts within one body.
Short coordinated imperatives include mutual honor, prayer and sharing with those in need. Hospitality concludes the sequence.
The initial command about persecutors leads into nonretaliation. The final appeal incorporates scriptural speech about vengeance and care for enemies.
The authority argument supplies reasons for subjection, then specifies taxes, revenue, respect and honor.
The debt metaphor introduces the command to love, reinforced by citations of commandments and the claim that love fulfills law.
The image of night giving way to day grounds behavioral exhortations and the call to put on Christ.
Food and days are named as matters of differing practice. Accountability to God grounds the appeal against contempt and judgment.
Paul distinguishes personal conviction about food from its effects on another. Peace, edification and conscience shape the closing appeal.
The stronger readers' obligations lead to a prayer for unity. The argument joins promises to Israel with a series of citations about the nations.
The mission rationale in 14–21 explains the travel plans in 22–24.
25 and 28 explain the itinerary. The named collection in 26 supplies the case for the argument in 27.
A proposed visit in 29 and a closing peace wish in 33 frame the appeal.
Phoebe's commendation includes direct instructions to receive and assist her. The exact sense of her titles requires separate Greek review.
1–2 are catalogued under the narrower Phoebe passage. 3–15 name particular coworkers and households. Verse 16 changes to a reciprocal instruction before closing with greetings.
Names, descriptions and greetings to particular coworkers provide evidence about their work. The sense of Junia's description in 7 requires separate study. No general office rule is stated.
Tertius identifies himself in verse 22. WEBP prints the grace blessing at 16:24 and the doxology at 14:24–26, with a placement note at 16:25. The doxology record retains conventional numbering.
Within the opening address, 1–3 link apostleship to hope, promise and proclamation. Verse 4 addresses Titus.
The purpose of leaving Titus in Crete is appointment of elders. The qualifications move from household conduct to teaching and responding to opponents in 9.

The ethnic slur in 12 is introduced as a local prophet's statement. The writer endorses it in 13 and directs correction. This is evidence of the letter's polemic, not evidence about the character of Cretans.
The address to Titus about sound teaching introduces directions specifically concerning older men in 2.
Older women are to teach younger women. The ensuing expectations concern marriage and household conduct; the passage gives no general definition of a teaching office.
The address to younger men and to Titus as a model precedes separate directions to enslaved people. Their conduct is connected with the public reputation of the teaching.
The writer presents grace as educating people for present conduct, links hope to Christ's self-giving, and closes by addressing Titus about the authority to teach and correct.
Civic conduct is followed by a first-person plural account of former wrongdoing and salvation through mercy. Verse 8 returns to insistence on good works.
Avoidance of disputes and the sequence of warnings precede the personal arrangements in 12–13. Verse 14 extends the concern about meeting needs to the community. Verse 15 closes the letter.
